title: Berlin woolwork
subtitle: The Victorian needlepoint tradition of charted designs in coloured wool
excerpt: Berlin woolwork is a style of Victorian needlepoint in which designs are worked from squared paper charts printed in Berlin from the 1820s onward. The charts matched specific wool colours to each square. Many classic needlepoint motifs come from Berlin work charts.
sourceNotes: Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), Berlin work entry. Weldon's Practical Needlework, Berlin work series (1880s). Mrs Beeton, Book of Needlework (1870), Project Gutenberg #16746.

glossaryTerms.definition: Victorian needlepoint worked from square-grid charts printed in Berlin, matched to specific dyed wool colours. Common on cushions, fire screens, and slippers from the 1820s through the 1880s.
Fine-staple wool from merino sheep, the basis of the tightly-spun Berlin wool used in Victorian woolwork. Softer and more lustrous than other wool types.

content.text: Berlin woolwork is the Victorian needlepoint tradition of working charted designs on canvas using specially dyed wool, with each square on the chart matched to a specific colour. The charts were printed in Berlin from the 1820s onward and sold across Europe. Roses, birds, parrots, classical figures, and geometric borders are among the most common subjects.

The designs are worked in continental or basketweave tent stitch on a canvas count suited to the size of the piece, typically 13 or 18 count. Many Berlin work pieces also use plush stitch, where loops are cut to give a velvety pile for flowers and animals.
Where to find historic Berlin work charts
charts in the public domain appear in library digital collections and the Internet Archive. Weldon's series and needlework books from the 1870s hold the most usable patterns.
The original Berlin wool was a fine, tightly spun

with very bright aniline dyes. Aniline dyes were new in the 1850s and 1860s; the vivid purples, magentas, and crimsons in Victorian pieces come from them. Modern Persian wool or tapestry wool in equivalent colour ranges works well for contemporary reproductions of the old charts.

Original Berlin work charts are squared-paper grids with a coloured or symbol-coded square for each stitch position. Each square is one tent stitch on the canvas. The chart often comes with a printed key matching each colour or symbol to a wool shade number. You
by counting squares on the chart and matching them to canvas holes, starting from a centre reference point.

Contemporary charted needlepoint follows the same system. A modern chart on squared paper reads exactly like a Berlin work chart. The difference is that modern charts often give a manufacturer's thread number (DMC, Anchor, or a wool brand shade number) rather than a Berlin shade match. The
technique is unchanged from the Victorian method.
